en: O beloved,

this summer season has arrived— the sun is fierce, the moon is desirable, the stores of water are diminished by constant bathing, it is delightful at the close of day, and the god of love has been subdued.
In the summer season, O beloved, the nights— marked by dark streaks where the moon has pierced them—
certainly delightful water-machines, rows of jewels, and fragrant sandalwood, all become objects of enjoyment for people.

In the pure stillness of the midnight, lovers enjoy the fragrant and enchanting palace terrace, the honey-like wine stirred by the breath from their beloved’s mouth, and songs from skilled lute-players that kindle the fire of passion.
With their rounded hips adorned with fine silken girdles, their breasts with pearl necklaces and sandalwood paste,
and their hair perfumed by bathing powders, women dispel the summer heat of lovers.
At every step, the feet of the women with shapely hips— adorned with anklets and dyed with the intense redness of lac-dye—
imitating the cries of swans, fill the hearts of people with passion.
Whose mind would not be filled with longing by breasts smeared with sandalwood paste, adorned with pearl necklaces as white as snow, and by hips graced with golden girdles? (Kalāvilāsa 1.6)
With the joints of their limbs covered in rising sweat, these women in the prime of youth now cast off their heavy garments and place thin silken cloths upon their high breasts.

Today, as if awakened from sleep, the God of Love is aroused by breezes arising from sandalwood water and fans, by the offering of the orb of her breasts adorned with pearl necklaces, and by the soft, melodious sounds of lute music.

Having gazed for a long time at the faces of women sleeping soundly in pleasure-groves and palaces during the nights, the moon surely becomes intensely eager; then, at the end of the night, he turns pale as if out of shame.
The earth, its circles of dust raised by unbearable winds and scorched by the heat of the fierce sun,
cannot even be looked upon by travelers whose minds are consumed by the fire of separation from their beloveds.

Severely tormented by the fierce heat and parched with great thirst, the deer, seeing the sky which resembles crushed collyrium, rushed into the midst of the forest thinking it to be water. (Kalpa Sūtra 1.11)
With their graceful movements and smiling, sidelong glances, the playful women instantly kindle the fire of love in the hearts of travelers, just as the nights, adorned by the beautiful moon, do.
Severely tormented by the rays of the sun and scorched on the path by the hot dust,
the serpent— with its face cast downward, moving in a winding course, and sighing repeatedly— sits beneath the peacock.
With his prowess and effort destroyed by great thirst, panting repeatedly with his mouth wide open,
the lord of beasts does not kill even the elephants nearby— his tongue lolling and the tips of his mane bristling.
Scorched by the rays of the sun, with sprays of water rising from their parched throats and afflicted by intense thirst,
the elephants seeking water do not fear even the lions.
With the rays of the sun acting like sacrificial fires, peacocks— whose bodies and minds were exhausted—
did not kill the serpent approaching them, even as its face was pressed against the circles of their plumage.
Digging up the dried mud of the lake along with its fragrant musta-grass,
the herd of boars, intensely scorched by the rays of the sun, seems to enter the very earth with its long rows of snouts.
Heated by Vivasvat, whose garland of rays is exceedingly sharp,
a frog leaps from the pond’s muddy water and settles beneath the parasol-like hood of a thirsty serpent.
The lake had its entire network of lotus stalks uprooted, its fish perished, and its cranes fled in haste;
it was turned into thick mud by elephants crowded together as they jostled one another.
The serpent, whose crest-jewel radiance is pierced by the sun’s light, who licks the air with his two flickering tongues,
and who is scorched by the heat of the poison-fire and the sun’s glare— though distressed by thirst, he does not kill the family of frogs.
With their snouts covered in froth and saliva, their red tongues lolling out, and their faces upturned,
herds of buffaloes emerged from mountain caves, agitated by thirst, and gazed longingly at the water.

The forest regions, where the sprouts of parched crops are being consumed by fierce forest fires, where withered leaves are tossed about by the force of harsh winds, and where the waters have been exhausted by the heat of the sun— these, when beheld from all sides, inspire great fear.
The flocks of birds sigh as they perch upon trees of withered leaves; the weary troop of monkeys seeks out the mountain’s thicket;
the herd of gayals wanders everywhere in search of water; and the straight-moving herd of śarabhas draws up water from the well.

The lands in every direction were swiftly scorched by a fire whose speed was increased by the force of a powerful wind, which possessed the brilliance of blooming saffron flowers and clear vermilion, and which was agitated as it embraced the tips of the creepers on the branches of the riverbanks.
Fanned by the wind, the forest fire blazes; it bursts forth with piercing sounds from the mountain caves and dry bamboo thickets.
Having gained strength as it spreads through the midst of the grass, the conflagration, upon reaching the edge of the forest, in an instant withers the herds of deer.

As if multiplied many times over, the fire—golden-hued within the hollows of the trees—blazes amidst the forests of *śālmali* trees; shaken by the wind, it wanders everywhere at the edge of the woods, leaping upon tall trees with their mature leaves and branches.
Elephants, gavayas, and lions, their bodies scorched by the fire, have abandoned their natural enmity and gathered together like friends;
emerging quickly from the thicket due to the exhaustion caused by the flames, they settle upon the river whose banks possess vast stretches of sand.

May your summer pass happily at night upon the roof of your palace, accompanied by amorous women, where the waters are strewn with lotus groves, which is delightful with the fragrance of trumpet-flowers, where the sprinkling of water is pleasant, and where the rays of the moon serve as a necklace. (Kalāvilāsa 1.28)

O beloved, the arrival of the rainy season has come like a king— possessing the lustre of an elephant in rut with water-bearing clouds as its spray, lightning as its banner, and the sound of thunderbolts as its drum; it is exalted in splendor and dear to those who long for love.

The sky was covered on all sides by clouds that in some places possessed the luster of the petals of intensely blue lotuses, in some places resembled heaps of split black collyrium, and in other places had the glow of the breasts of pregnant women.
Entreated by flocks of cātaka birds distressed by thirst,
the clouds— laden with heavy water, raining down many torrents, and possessing sounds that delight the ear— proceed slowly.
The clouds, sounding like thunder and drums and bearing Indra’s bow with its streaks of lightning,
violently pierce the hearts of travelers with their fierce arrows of falling, razor-sharp raindrops.
Covered with sprouts of grass resembling split beryl and with the upturned leaves of *kandalī* plants,
the earth shines like a beautiful woman adorned with gems other than white, thanks to the *indragopaka* insects.

Today, the flock of peacocks has begun its dance— ever charming with their cries, eager for the festival, adorned by their outspread and expansive plumage, and agitated by hurried embraces and kisses.
Felling the trees on their banks with their turbid waters of increased velocity,
the rivers flow swiftly toward the ocean like wicked women who, through the infatuation of their nature, destroy those around them.

The forests of the Vindhya range captivate the mind, carpeted with heaps of grass from which tender sprouts have emerged, marked by the dark wounds made by the mouths of does, and adorned with trees bearing rising shoots.
The sandy woodland, strewn on all sides with deer whose faces are graced by trembling blue-lotus eyes and who are overcome with fear,
excites longing in the heart.
Even on nights made thick with darkness by clouds that roar incessantly and loudly,
women going to meet their lovers proceed out of passion, their paths revealed by the flashes of lightning.
With their breasts emitting deep and formidable roars and with flashes of lightning that greatly agitate the mind,
women embrace their lovers incessantly upon the bed, even those who have committed offenses against them.
With the lovely sprouts of their bimba-fruit lips drenched by drops of water from the blue-lotus eyes,
and with their garlands, ornaments, and unguents cast aside, the women stood there, hopeless for those who had gone abroad.
Pale yellowish-white, mixed with insects, dust, and grass, gliding along with crooked movements like a serpent,
and watched with trepidation by swarms of frogs, the new rainwater flows toward the lowlands.

Leaving behind the lotus pond whose leaves and flowers have withered, the bees—whose humming is melodious to the ear—are eager; yet, deluded by the hope of fresh blue lotuses, they fall upon the circles of plumage of the dancing peacocks.
The temples of the rutting forest elephants, resounding repeatedly with cries like those of fresh rain clouds,
possess the luster of stainless blue lotuses and are drenched with ichor that swarms with bees.
The mountains, their rocks kissed by clouds white as blue lotuses, covered on all sides by waterfalls,
and crowded with peacocks who have begun to dance, generate a sense of longing.

Shaking the groves of kadamba, sarja, arjuna, and ketakī trees and scented by their blossoms, which breeze—cooled by contact with water-laden clouds and carrying fine droplets—does not fill one with longing? 2.17.
With their hair hanging down over the slopes of their hips, with fragrant flowers worn as ear-ornaments,
with breasts adorned by necklaces, and with faces accompanied by wine, women produce delight in those filled with passion.
They carry, they rain, they roar, they shine, they exert themselves, they dance, and they take refuge:
the rivers, the clouds, the rutting elephants, the forest edges, the peacocks separated from their beloveds, and the monkeys.
Adorned with streaks of lightning and Indra’s bow, the clouds hang heavy with water;
and women, radiant with girdles and jeweled earrings, simultaneously captivate the hearts of travelers.
Today the women wear on their heads garlands fashioned from *kadamba*, *navakesara*, and *ketakī* flowers,
and they wear ear-ornaments (*avataṃsaka*) arranged according to their own desire, made from the blossoms of the *kakubha* tree.
With their limbs anointed with black aloe and flowing sandalwood paste, and their tresses made fragrant with flower ornaments, the women,
hearing the sound of the clouds at nightfall, hasten from their elders' houses into their bedchambers.
With their dark-blue petals like blue water-lilies, lofty yet bowed by the weight of water, swaying gently as shaken by a soft breeze,
and adorned with rainbows, the clouds have, as it were, stolen away the hearts of the wives of travelers who are distressed by separation from them.
The forest interior seems to rejoice with *kadamba* trees that have burst into bloom on all sides, and it dances as if with trees whose branches sway in the wind;
the end of the forest, its heat severed by the sprinkling of fresh water, seems to break into laughter with the needle-like filaments of the *ketakī*.

This rainy season, like a lover, fashions for the young women a bakula garland upon their heads combined with jasmine flowers and blossoming yūthikā buds, as well as ear-ornaments made of blooming fresh kadamba flowers. 2.25.
With their high, excellent breasts, the women bear strings of pearls; with their broad hips, they wear thin white silk garments;
and with their waists, marked by graceful folds, they display the lines of body hair rising from being sprinkled with fresh raindrops.
Acquiring coolness from contact with fresh drops of water, causing the trees bent under the weight of blossoms to dance,
and generating a lovely fragrance through the pollen of *ketakī* flowers, the wind steals away the hearts of those who dwell abroad.
Thinking, "This lofty mountain is our refuge for those weighed down by the burden of water," the clouds, themselves bent low by their own moisture,
seem to refresh the Vindhya range— whose heat has been generated by the exceedingly harsh flames of the summer fire— with their showers.
Charming with its many virtues, captivating the hearts of women, the friend of trees, branches, and creepers, and remaining ever-unchanging—
may this rainy season, which is the very life-breath of living beings, bestow upon you benefits that generally accord with your desires.

The third canto: Autumn has arrived, lovely as a bride, with the *kāśa* grass for her silken garment, beautiful faces of full-blown lotuses, charming with the tinkling of anklets in the form of the cries of intoxicated swans,
and her slender body bent down by rows of ripening rice.
The earth was whitened by kāśa grass, the nights by the cool-rayed moon, the waters of the rivers by swans, the lakes by white lotuses,
the forest edges by saptacchada trees bent under the weight of their blossoms, and the groves by mālatī jasmine.
With girdles of shimmering, charming minnows for their waist-bands, and rows of white birds standing on the banks for their pearl necklaces,
the rivers— possessing the curves of broad sandy banks as their hips— now move slowly like intoxicated women.
In some places, the sky is observed to be fanned by hundreds of clouds— white as silver, conch shells, and lotus stalks— which, having shed their water,
move swiftly in the wind due to their lightness, like a king being fanned by hundreds of whisks.
The sky, lovely with the splendor of a mass of crushed collyrium, and the earth, reddened by the pollen of bandhūka flowers;
and the embankments, their surfaces covered with ripening *kalama* rice—whom among the youths on earth would these not fill with longing?

Whose heart is not rent asunder by the *kovidāra* tree, whose most beautiful upper branches are tossed by a gentle breeze, whose tips of tender sprouts are thick with emerging blossoms, and from which the outpouring of honey is drunk by intoxicated bees?
Bearing the finest ornaments of the host of stars, her face like the moon released from the confinement of clouds,
and wearing the spotless silken garment of moonlight, the night advances daily toward fullness like a young woman.
The rivers, their garlands of waves unagitated by *kāraṇḍava* ducks, their banks crowded with flocks of *kādamba* geese and *sārasa* cranes,
and reddened by the pollen of lotuses, bring joy to the people on all sides with the cries of swans.
A festival for the eyes, a garland of rays that captivates the heart, a source of delight raining down cool spray—
yet the moon excessively consumes the bodies of women whose limbs are wounded by the poison-tipped arrows of separation from their husbands.
Making the clusters of rice stalks bowed down by the weight of their fruit tremble, causing the excellent trees bent with blossoms to dance,
and shaking the lotus pond filled with blooming lotuses, the wind violently agitates the minds of those who are deficient.
Adorned by pairs of intoxicated swans, graced with clear, blooming lotuses and water-lilies,
and possessing garlands of ripples raised by the gentle breezes of dawn, these lakes suddenly stir the longing of the heart.
The bow of Indra has vanished within the bellies of the clouds; the lightning, that banner of the sky, does not flash today.
The cranes do not stir the heavens with the wind of their wings, nor do the peacocks gaze at the sky with upturned faces.
Abandoning the peacocks who have ceased their dance, Madana approaches the swans with their sweet songs;
leaving behind the kadamba, kuṭaja, arjuna, sarja, and nīpa trees, the splendor of the blossoming flowers has reached the saptacchadas.
The pleasure groves, enchanting with the fragrance of *śephālikā* flowers, resounded with the cries of flocks of birds resting at ease,
and possessing the lotus-eyes of does standing at their borders, stir the hearts of men with longing.
Repeatedly shaking the white, red, and blue lotuses, and having acquired an even greater coolness through contact with them,
the breeze at dawn— fanning the dew-drops clinging to the tips of the leaves— arouses intense longing.
The borders of the fields, their ground covered with abundant harvests of rice, beautified by numerous herds of cattle standing at ease,
and made resonant by flocks of swans and cranes, produce delight in men.
The graceful gait of the women was surpassed by swans; the radiance of their moon-like faces by blooming lotuses;
their eyes, sweet with passion, by blue water-lilies; and their beautiful play of eyebrows by slender, rippling waves.
The dark creepers, with their tender shoots bent down by the weight of blossoms, steal away the beauty of women’s arms adorned with ornaments;
and the fresh mālatī, radiant with the lovely flowers of the aśoka, takes away the splendor of the moon-like smile brightened by the luster of teeth.
The women fill their hair—extremely thick, dark blue, and with curled ends—with fresh mālatī flowers;
and upon their ears, adorned with excellent golden earrings, they place various blue lotuses.
Today, with joyful hearts, women adorn their circular breasts with necklaces and sandalwood paste, their broad hips with girdles of tinkling bells, and their lotus-feet with exquisite anklets.

The cloudless sky, strewn with the moon and stars, bears a beauty of surpassing form, resembling bodies of water filled with blooming white lotuses, inhabited by royal swans, and adorned with water possessing the luster of emeralds.
In autumn, cool breezes blow from contact with the white water-lilies; the quarters of the sky are delightful, their masses of clouds having vanished.
The waters are free from turbidity, the earth has its mud dried up, and the sky is variegated with stars and possesses the moon of stainless rays.

Other young women, charming with lotus-like hands, their hands clasped by their lovers, and whose faces surpass the moon, mostly go to their homes adorned with fragrant flowers; having abandoned their passion for music, they do so primarily because of the powerful influence of love.

In the midst of the night during autumn, young women, accompanied by their virtuous female friends, display with great delight the playful charms of amorous passion; with their incomparable facial expressions, they indicate the diversion of the god of the five arrows and manifest their joys.
Oppressed by the rays of the sun at dawn, the lotus, which resembles the face of a beautiful young woman, now expands;
yet the night-lily, too, withers as the lunar disc sets, like the laughter of women when their beloveds have gone abroad.
Having perceived the beauty of their dark eyes in the blue lotuses, the sound of their tinkling golden girdles in the calls of intoxicated swans,
and the lovely splendor of their lips in the bandhujīva flowers, the traveler now weeps with a bewildered heart for his beloveds.
Having abandoned the splendor of the moon from the faces of women, the desirable speech of swans from their jeweled anklets,
and the beauty of the bandhūka flower from their enchanting lips, the auspicious glory of autumn’s arrival departs for some unknown place.
With a face like a blooming lotus, eyes like full-blown blue water-lilies, and wearing garments as white as a fresh autumn sky,
possessing the radiant beauty of the night-lily, may this Autumn bestow upon my heart the supreme joy of a passionate woman in her intoxication.
This winter season has arrived, lovely with the emergence of new sprouts and crops, with lodhra trees in full bloom and rice fully ripened;
it is the time when lotuses have faded and frost falls down.
The orb-like breasts of playful women, graced with swelling bosoms, are adorned with captivating necklaces white as sandalwood paste, resembling frost, jasmine, and the moon.
Bracelets and armlets no longer cling to the arms of playful women; fresh silk garments no longer rest upon their hips, nor fine muslin upon their full breasts.
The young women do not adorn their hips with girdles variegated with gold and jewels,
nor do they grace their lotus-like feet— possessing the luster of lotuses— with anklets that emulate the cry of swans.

With their limbs anointed with *kālīyaka* paste and adorned with decorative leaf-patterns, and their lotus-faces perfumed with black aloe-wood incense, women prepare themselves for the festival of love.
The young women, their faces pale and thin from the exhaustion of passion, yet having attained the height of joy,
do not laugh aloud as they behold their lower lips, bitten by the tips of teeth and being pressed.
Having attained the beauty of her full breasts and broad chest, the winter season, distressed by the pressure of those limbs,
seems to wail at dawn through the falling drops of frost clinging to the tips of blades of grass.
The borders of the fields, strewn with abundant harvests of rice, adorned by herds of female deer, and made resonant by the enchanting cries of cranes, stir the heart with longing.
Lakes adorned with blossoming blue lotuses, graced by intoxicated kadamba birds,
possessing clear waters and cool temperatures, captivate the hearts of men.
Beholding the path whose waters had been utterly exhausted, the fawn-eyed women bore their husbands who were weary from travel; looking back at them, they seemed to awaken their own longings.
Constantly shaken by winds cold as if born from snow, the *priyaṅgu* creeper ripens; separated from her beloved, she turns pale like a graceful woman parted from her lover.
With faces fragrant with the scent of flower-liquor, their bodies perfumed by the breath of their sighs,
people steeped in the essence of passion lie sleeping, their limbs entwined with one another.

The merciless enjoyment of sexual pleasure by young women is indicated by their lips marked with the signs of bitten teeth, and by their breasts bearing the impressions made by the tips of fingers. (Kalāvilāsa 4.13)
A certain woman, her hand resting on a mirror, adorns the lotus of her face in the morning sunlight;
she draws back and gazes at her lower lip, its essence sipped by her beloved and marked by the indentations of his teeth.
Another woman, her body exhausted by the fatigue of unrestrained lovemaking, her lotus-eyes bloodshot from staying awake all night,
her beautiful mass of hair disheveled and falling over her shoulders, falls asleep as she is warmed by the soft rays of the sun.

Other young women, their slender bodies bent under the weight of full and elevated breasts, remove from their heads the fragrant garlands of offerings that have been enjoyed, and arrange their thick, dark blue tresses.

Beholding her body enjoyed by her beloved, she was filled with joy; with the lovely beauty of her lips restored, her limbs marked by nail-scratches, and her eyes curved by locks of dark, beautiful hair hanging down, she put on her bodice.

Other beautiful women, having long since succumbed to exhaustion from the fatigue of amorous play, their slender bodies now limp, with the hair on their thighs and the curves of their breasts bristling with thrill, apply fragrant unguents.

May this snowy season, delightful with its many qualities, captivating to the hearts of women, with village boundaries bustling with ripening rice, where the frost has fallen and the cry of the cranes serves as song, grant you happiness.
The fifth canto:

O fair-limbed one, hear now of the season called Śiśira (winter), which covers the earth with thickets of ripened rice and sugarcane, which is resplendent with the cries of krauñca birds perched here and there, which is free from excessive passion, and which is dear to young women.
In this season, the interior of houses with their windows closed, fires, the rays of the sun,
heavy garments, and even young women lose their desirability for people.
Neither sandalwood cool as moonbeams, nor palace rooftops bright as the autumn moon, nor winds cooled by dense frost can delight the heart of people at this time. (Kalpanāmaṇḍitikā 5.3)
The nights, cooled by the falling of masses of snow and further chilled by the rays of the moon,
adorned with the lovely ornaments of the pale white clusters of stars, are no longer fit for people to enjoy.
Having taken up betel, ointments, and garlands, their lotus-faces fragrant with the scent of flower-liquor,
the eager women enter the bedchamber, which is perfumed by the smoke of choice black aloe-wood incense.

Beholding their husbands— who had repeatedly committed offenses, were now trembling with fear, whose minds were clouded by terror, yet who longed for sexual union— the women, intoxicated with passion, forgot those transgressions.
Having been enjoyed for a long time without mercy during the long nights by youths of excessive desire,
the women in the prime of their youth now wander slowly at the end of the night, their bodies weary from exhaustion.
With breasts pressed by charming bodices and thighs adorned with crimson silk garments,
the women— whose hair was interspersed with flowers within— seemed to be adorning the arrival of winter.
With their chests pressed by playful women whose breasts are tawny with the hue of saffron and whose youthful warmth is so pleasant to experience,
lovers sleep, overcoming the cold.

At night, joyful women together with their lovers drink the most excellent intoxicating wine—a captivating drink that awakens the pleasure of love and causes blue lotuses to tremble at their fragrant sighs. *Kāvyamīmāṃsā* 5.10.

At dawn, a certain woman, her pride and passion departed, having pressed her firm breasts together through her husband’s embrace, gazes upon her own body enjoyed by her beloved; smiling, she leaves the bedchamber for another room.

Another passionate woman, heavy-hipped, deep-navelled, and slender-waisted, bearing a mass of hair fragrant with the scent of aloe-wood incense, its tips curled and its flower-garlands fallen away, leaves her bed at dawn, possessing a lovely beauty.

Today at dawn, the women stand within their homes like personified goddesses of fortune, with faces as lovely as golden lotuses, with beautiful copper-red lips, with eyes reddish at the corners and resting against the slopes of their ears, and with locks of hair clinging to their shoulders.
Afflicted by the weight of their broad hips, with waists slightly bent and moving very slowly due to the exhaustion from the burden of their breasts,
other young women quickly cast off their nocturnal attire suited for the time of love and donned garments appropriate for the day.
Beholding the regions of their breasts marked by nail-prints, touching the tips of their sprout-like lower lips bitten by teeth,
and adorning their faces at the time of sunrise, the young women bring joy with their attire suited for their desired dalliance.
Abounding in preparations of molasses, delightful with sweet rice and sugarcane, characterized by intense amorous play and the pride of awakened passion—
may this winter season, which causes the burning torment of hearts for those separated from their beloveds, ever bring you prosperity.
The sixth canto:

[Description of Spring] O beloved, the warrior Spring has arrived to pierce the hearts of those engaged in amorous play; his sharp arrows are the sprouts of blossoming mango trees, and the humming of swarms of bees is his vibrating bowstring.
The trees are in bloom, the waters are filled with lotuses, women are full of desire, and the breeze is fragrant;
the evenings are pleasant and the days are delightful—everything is more beautiful in spring when one’s beloved is present.

In the springtime, women make their mansions cool with slight frost, perfume them, and adorn their beautiful hair with *campaka* flowers; they also decorate their breasts with lovely blossoms and pearl necklaces.
Spring bestows an essence of beauty upon the waters of the ponds, upon women adorned with jeweled girdles, upon the splendors of the moon, upon young women,
and upon mango trees laden with blossoms.
The rounded hips of the playful women are adorned with fine silk garments reddened by safflower dye,
while their orb-like breasts are embellished with thin cloths pale with the hue of saffron.
The fresh *karṇikāra* flower becomes worthy upon their ears; the blue *aśoka* upon their flickering locks;
and the blossoming, new *mallikā* flower attains its splendor upon the womenfolk.
Necklaces moist with white sandalwood rest upon their breasts, bracelets and armlets cling to their arms,
and girdles settle upon the hips of those broad-hipped women whose minds are afflicted by the god of love.
Upon the faces of the playful women, which resemble golden lotuses adorned with leaf-patterns,
the arrival of perspiration spreads, charming amidst the jewels like a cluster of pearls.
Sighing as their limbs loosen their bonds and become agitated by the god of love,
women now become truly eager for their lovers who are standing nearby.
The bodiless god of love makes the limbs of young women thin, pale, languid with passion, repeatedly intent on yawning, and overflowing with a flurry of beauty.
During the day, people long for the shade of trees; at night, they likewise desire the rays of the moon.
They go to their mansions to sleep in pleasant coolness, and because of that coolness, they embrace their beloveds tightly.

Today the bodiless god of love resides in many forms among women: restless in their eyes, languid with wine in their cheeks, pale in their breasts, firm in their bosoms, sunken in their waists, and full in their hips.
Love rendered the limbs of young women languid with the grace of sleep, their speech slightly slurred by wine,
and their glances crooked with the knitting of eyebrows.
Sandalwood paste, anointed with *priyaṅgu*, *kālīyaka*,
and saffron, and mixed with musk, is smeared upon their fair breasts by the playful women who are languid with passion.
Quickly casting off heavy garments, people whose limbs are languid with the intoxication of passion don light clothes dyed with lac-dye and perfumed with the smoke of fragrant black aloe-wood.
Intoxicated by the juice of the mango tree, the male cuckoo, thrilled with passion, kisses his beloved;
and this bee, dwelling within the lotus and warbling, offers sweet flattery to his mate.
The mango trees, their beautiful branches in bloom and bent low under clusters of copper-red shoots,
being shaken by the breeze, stir the longing minds of women with intense yearning.
Bearing clusters of blossoms with young shoots, copper-red like the hue of coral from their very roots,
the Ashoka trees cause the hearts of those in the bloom of youth to be filled with sorrow when they behold them.

With their lovely flowers being kissed by intoxicated bees, and their soft young shoots drooping when stirred by the gentle breeze, the young *atimukta* creepers, upon being beheld, suddenly arouse longing in the hearts of lovers.

O beloved, seeing the supreme beauty of the fresh clusters of *kurabaka* blossoms, which possess a luster like that of a lovely woman’s face, whose heart would not be pained by the falling of Cupid’s arrows, for it belongs to one who possesses a sensitive soul? (Kalāvilāsa 6.20)
Covered everywhere with groves of *kiṃśuka* trees— bending under the weight of their blossoms and shaken by the wind like blazing fires—
the earth, now fully invested by the season of spring, shines like a young bride clad in crimson silk.
What has not been surpassed by the *kiṃśuka* flowers, which possess the luster of a parrot’s beak? What has not been consumed by the *karṇikāra* blossoms?
Yet this cuckoo, with its sweet notes, strikes down the hearts of young men already fixed upon fair-faced women.
With the sweet-voiced male cuckoos warbling with joy and the bees humming their intoxicated, melodious songs,
the hearts of the young brides— even while in their family homes— were instantly made agitated, filled with bashfulness, and overcome by modesty.

In spring, as the fall of frost has ceased, the wind blows auspiciously, shaking the branches of flowering mango trees and spreading the songs of the cuckoo in all directions; it steals away the hearts of men.
The enchanting groves, illuminated by flower-pots as bright as the playful smiles of young wives,
captivate even the mind of a sage whose passions have ceased, let alone the hearts of youths already stained by desire.

In the month of Madhu, women— with golden girdles dangling, pearl necklaces clinging to their breasts, and slender bodies made supple by the pride of Kandarpa— forcibly steal the hearts of men with the sweet songs of cuckoos and bees.
Seeing those mountains adorned with various trees of lovely blossoms, their slopes filled with the joyful warbling of cuckoos,
and their rocky surfaces covered with networks of *śaileya* plants, every person experiences great delight.
Closing his eyes, weeping, falling into grief, covering his nose with his hand, and crying out loudly—
thus does a traveler, his mental state distressed by separation from his beloved, react upon seeing mango trees in full bloom.
Delightful with the songs of cuckoos and intoxicated bees, and with blossoming mango and karṇikāra trees,
the month of flowers pierces the hearts of proud women with its arrows as if they were exceedingly sharp, for the purpose of inflaming the god of love.

Beholding on the road ahead the blossoming mango trees, which shed heaps of flowers possessing the luster of beautiful gold when shaken by gentle breezes, the traveler— though his body is already emaciated— falls into a swoon from the strikes of the arrows of Love.

Now, spring mocks the speech of amorous women with the sweet songs of cuckoos, their smiles with the radiance of jasmine flowers, and the beauty of their sprout-like hands with foliage the hue of coral. *Kalpadrukośa* 6.31.
With faces as lovely as golden lotuses and pale cheeks, with necklaces placed upon their chests and the space between their breasts moist with sandalwood paste, noble women—
bowed by the weight of their breasts— desire the peaceful lords of sages with glances full of passion-born coquetry.

The lotus-face fragrant with honey, the eyes copper-hued like *lodhra* flowers, the lovely mass of hair filled with fresh *kurabaka* blossoms, the pair of heavy breasts, and likewise the orb of the hips—does all this not now serve to incite passion in women? (Kalāvilāsa 6.33)
The hearts of the high-minded women were shaken by breezes scented with blossoming mango trees,
and by the warbling of intoxicated cuckoos and the songs of bees, both of which were pleasing to the ear.
The lovely hour of twilight with the radiance of the full moon, the cry of the male cuckoo, the fragrant breeze,
the humming of swarms of intoxicated bees, and the drinking of wine at night— all this is an elixir for the god whose weapon is the flower.

May the arrival of spring—the beloved of Madana—grant you blessings until the end of the aeon; he whose sweet lower lip is fashioned of red Aśoka flowers, whose voice is the sound of intoxicated bees, whose mass of teeth is as pure as a cluster of Kunda blossoms, whose face is a full-blown lotus, who possesses a gentle breeze fragrant with the scent of mango, and who is the preceptor for the initiation into the erotic sentiment.
Fanned by the Malaya breeze, delightful with the warbling of cuckoos, having acquired a continuous flow of fragrance from the sprinkling of fragrant honey,
and surrounded on all sides by various swarms of bees— may this spring, the most excellent season, bring you happiness.

May that bodiless Spring, the conqueror of the world, bestow upon you manifold blessings— he whose arrow is the lovely mango blossom, whose bow is the excellent *kiṃśuka* flower, whose bowstring is the swarm of bees, whose spotless umbrella is the white-rayed moon, whose rutting elephant is the Malaya breeze, and whose bards are the cuckoos.
